clue.text: Brand accepts plan backing guarantee (4,4)

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in, and a word that takes another in has to open up and hold it.
A thing that is backing is travelling rear-end first, so the letters of the word beside it arrive in reverse.

blocks.note: a car's brand is its make
a crafty plan is a RUSE, written back to front

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a company standing behind a scheme. The wordplay needs 'brand' as a noun, and that noun then splits open before its last letter to let the ruse in.
explanation.definitionFit: guarantee → MAKE SURE: to guarantee an outcome is to make sure of it, a two-word verb phrase standing in for the single verb.

clue.text: Start to watch broadband supplier’s strand (4)

indicators.note: 'Start to' points at the beginning of the action named next, so only the opening letter of that word is wanted.

blocks.note: the first letter of watch
an internet service provider is the firm that sells you broadband

explanation.walkthrough: ISP is worth banking: setters reach for it whenever broadband, the web or a connection turns up, and three of the four letters arrive in one go.
explanation.definitionFit: strand → WISP: a wisp is a single thin strand of hair, smoke or straw — one trailing piece rather than a bundle.

clue.text: Subsection of secret summons turned around rally (6)

indicators.note: A subsection is a piece cut out of something longer, which is the instruction: take a run of letters from inside the words that follow.
Turned around means facing the other way, so that run of letters has to be read from its far end back.

blocks.note: secRET SUMmons carries RETSUM, which reads the other way as the answer

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden run almost always straddles a word boundary, because your eye reads whole words and skips the join — and here it is buried backwards as well.
explanation.definitionFit: rally → MUSTER: to rally troops is to muster them, both verbs meaning to gather scattered people into one body ready for action.

clue.text: One who keeps quiet before the Guardian’s outcry (7)

indicators.note: 'Before' is positional, not temporal: the piece it follows is laid down first and the next one comes after it.

blocks.note: someone who clams up gives nothing away
the paper printing this puzzle calls what belongs to it ours

explanation.walkthrough: A paper naming itself in its own crossword is a Guardian regular — read the italicised title as the word the paper would use for its own property.
explanation.definitionFit: outcry → CLAMOUR: a clamour is the loud protesting din a crowd raises, which is exactly the public complaint an outcry names.

clue.text: A female or male tennis icon? (4)

blocks.note: the article is taken as it stands
'female' is a common stand-in for the three-letter subject pronoun

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the sex change: two words for a woman spell a man. Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975 and has New York's main court named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: male tennis icon → ASHE: definition by example, naming one particular great of the game rather than giving a synonym for a player.

clue.text: Chamber’s diet for those chosen (10)

blocks.note: the debating chamber where a country's laws are argued
a diet is a formal assembly — Japan still calls its own one — and its members are the elected

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'diet' as food. In politics a diet is an assembly, so both halves of the clue are describing the same institution from different angles.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves name the assembly: it is the chamber a nation debates in, and it is the diet — the sitting body — made up of those the voters chose.

clue.text: Late meeting of party in bishop’s office (6)

indicators.note: 'In' is doing spatial work rather than joining a phrase: what precedes it goes inside what follows.

blocks.note: a bishop's office and district is his see
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' is the obituary sense — the late Mr Jones — so this is a meeting with the dead, not one that runs past six o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Late meeting → SEANCE: a sitting at which a medium tries to contact the dead, so the gathering really is with those who have died.

clue.text: It’s normal for holiday at Legoland at the outset to involve a little something for everyone (8)

indicators.note: At the outset means right at the start, so each word it looks back at surrenders only its opening letter.
To involve something is to have it inside you, so the letters already found close around what comes next.

blocks.clueFragment: holiday at Legoland at the outset
blocks.note: the opening letters of Holiday At Legoland
a little of something is a bit of it
a U certificate marks a film as universal, passed for everyone

explanation.walkthrough: The family outing is decoration — all the clue wants from Legoland is a letter. Bank the U: a U certificate film is the one anybody is allowed to watch.
explanation.definitionFit: normal → HABITUAL: something done by habit, so regularly that it counts as the normal thing for that person to do.

clue.text: See 10
Spooner’s expensive rendezvous with The Blob? (4,5)

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so naming him is the instruction to swap them over.

blocks.note: expensive is steep, and Spooner takes its ST away in exchange for a D
a rendezvous is a date, and it picks up the ST that steep gave up

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Blob' is the political jibe for the permanent officialdom ministers say frustrates them; the question mark admits it is a nickname rather than a dictionary word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blob → DEEP STATE: two sneering names for the same thing, the unelected machinery said to run a country whoever wins the election.

clue.text: I tremble in feverish place where the fuel runs out? (10)

definitions.text: place where the fuel runs out

indicators.note: Feverish is the shivering, restless state of a fever, and letters that cannot keep still will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: ten letters of I TREMBLE IN, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The shivering and the mountain cold pull the same way, which is the misdirection. 'Fuel' here means firewood, and trees are what stop at that altitude.
explanation.definitionFit: place where the fuel runs out → TIMBERLINE: above that altitude no trees grow, so a climber gathering wood to burn finds nothing left.

clue.text: Relish killing (6)

blocks.note: the slang sense of falling on something with great appetite, as in a familiar phrase about craving a curry
the crime itself, one person unlawfully killing another

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses, and a nastier surface than either deserves. It is also one of this grid's collective nouns — crows come in one.
explanation.definitionFit: The plain sense is the crime, killing someone unlawfully; the slang sense is the appetite of 'I could murder a pint', devouring something with relish.

clue.text: Thwart fickle rule in gear shift? (10)

indicators.note: A fickle person will not stay as they were a minute ago, and letters that will not stay put have to be rearranged.

blocks.note: to derail a plan is to thwart it
the four letters of RULE, shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: The bicycle sense is the surprise: a derailleur is the arm that lifts the chain from one sprocket to the next, borrowed whole from French.
explanation.definitionFit: gear shift → DERAILLEUR: the technical name for the bicycle mechanism that shifts the chain across the sprockets, so the everyday phrase names the part.

clue.text: Open to the elements, caps missing, air processor burned (8)

indicators.note: A cap sits on top, so a word that has lost its cap has lost the letter at its front.

blocks.note: a lung processes air, and the L on top of it goes
burned is blazed, and the B on top of it goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Caps' is plural, and that is the step people miss: one instruction beheads both words, which is why the second half looks nothing like the answer at first.
explanation.definitionFit: Open to the elements → UNGLAZED: a window or frame with no glass fitted, so nothing stands between the room and the weather.

clue.text: Sport cut short leg (3)

indicators.note: To cut something short is to lop the end off it, so the final letter of the word never arrives.

blocks.note: a sport is a game, docked of its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: A gam is also a school of whales, so this one is quietly part of the grid's collection as well as being music-hall slang.
explanation.definitionFit: leg → GAM: dated slang, chiefly American, for a person's leg — a word of the music halls that survives mainly in crosswords.

clue.text: Unravel slam point (7)

blocks.note: to slam a film in a review is to decry it
PT is the standard abbreviation for point, as on a chart

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slam' invites you to think of doors and dunks; the wanted sense is the reviewer's. With no indicator anywhere, the two pieces simply sit end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Unravel → DECRYPT: to decrypt a message is to unravel it, turning a scrambled cipher back into sense the way you unpick a knot.

clue.text: Hope to God every third letter appears in books made to order (3)

definitions.note: The definition names what comes off the press rather than the process: POD is print on demand, a way of making books, and the clue defines it by its output.

indicators.note: This is a counting instruction rather than a description: walk through the preceding words in threes and keep only the one you land on.

blocks.note: HOPETOGOD falls into HOP, ETO, GOD, and the third letter of each group is what is kept

explanation.walkthrough: Print on demand is the publishing trade's own abbreviation: a title is printed only once somebody has bought a copy, so no stock sits in a warehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: books made to order → POD: print on demand, the trade's term for running off a copy only after it has been ordered.

clue.text: Mammoth setter’s crew stripped user (7)

indicators.note: Something stripped has had its outside removed, so the word beside it loses the letters at each end.

blocks.note: the setter speaks as I, so the setter is becomes I'M
a ship's crew is its men
uSEr with its outside letters taken off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' is the Guardian solver's daily bread — the setter is I, so the possessive is I'M. Mammoth is the adjective here, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mammoth → IMMENSE: used as an adjective, mammoth simply means huge, and immense is the plain synonym for something vast in scale.

clue.text: Smartening up University College in April and May (8)

indicators.note: 'In' is a placement here, not a preposition of the surface: the two abbreviations go inside, not alongside.

blocks.note: both months fall in the same season
U is the usual abbreviation, as in a degree from U of London
C abbreviates college in the names of institutions

explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters make University College look like one place in London, which is the misdirection: the clue wants an initial from each.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartening up → SPRUCING: to spruce something up is to tidy it into a neat, well-turned-out state, and both words are -ing forms.

clue.text: Offensive in the armed forces? (7)

definitions.note: The second definition is a phrase where the answer is an adjective: the setter is reading 'civil' as civilian, so somebody serving in the forces is literally un-civil.

blocks.note: the everyday sense — rude, discourteous, giving offence
a soldier is not a civilian and not in the civil service, so not civil

explanation.walkthrough: Everything hangs on which 'civil' you hear: polite in one half, civilian in the other. The question mark is the setter owning up to the second one.
explanation.definitionFit: Offensive → UNCIVIL means rude or discourteous; the forces half plays on the other sense of civil, the one that means civilian rather than polite.

clue.text: Walked free in road house (8)

definitions.note: 'Walked' serves as both past tense and past participle, and only the participle sense matches: you have walked, you have stridden.

indicators.note: 'In' says the piece before it drops inside, landing between the two short words that follow.

blocks.note: street shortens to ST on any address
to be free of something is to be rid of it
a den is a small private room in a house

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'roadhouse' as one word, which is the trap — road and house are clued separately, and the participle is one solvers forget exists.
explanation.definitionFit: Walked → STRIDDEN: the past participle of stride, which is walking with long purposeful steps, so it fills the same slot after 'has'.

clue.text: Some leaderless after god proving hard to please (6)

indicators.note: A leaderless group has lost the one at its head, so the word gives up its first letter.
'After' fixes the order against the surface: the piece named first ends up behind the one named second.

blocks.note: Thor, the Norse god of thunder
some is any, which loses the A at its head

explanation.walkthrough: Norse gods are crossword furniture — THOR, ODIN, LOKI all fit tight spaces. Here the god's name is laid down first even though the clue mentions him second.
explanation.definitionFit: hard to please → THORNY: a thorny character is prickly to deal with, snagging on whatever is offered, so nothing you bring them is ever right.

clue.text: Sew up ruptured uterus (6)

indicators.note: A ruptured thing has burst apart, and once the letters are in pieces they can be put back in any order.

blocks.note: the six letters of UTERUS, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Surgical from end to end: what ruptures is the very thing you stitch, so fodder and definition belong to one scene rather than fighting each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Sew up → SUTURE: the surgeon's verb for stitching a wound closed, the technical word sitting under the everyday phrase.

clue.text: Ask Einstein to include networks (6)

indicators.note: To include is to contain already, so the letters are sitting inside the words as written rather than being built.

blocks.note: aSK EINStein runs the letters straight through the gap between the words

explanation.walkthrough: A famous name is where setters like to bury things: you read Einstein as a person and never as six letters carried over from the word before.
explanation.definitionFit: networks → SKEINS: a skein is a loose coil of yarn, and the word carries over to any tangle of interwoven lines or connections.

clue.text: Ten solutions may provide tonic with novel clues (10,5)

definitions.note: The definition points outside its own clue: ten of this puzzle's other answers belong to the class named, so the phrase defines the answer by what the grid holds.

indicators.note: 'May provide' offers the words that follow as raw material — they can yield something else, so they are not to be read as they stand.

blocks.note: the fifteen letters of TONIC, NOVEL and CLUES, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Ten of the other answers here are the crowd word for some creature — owls, crows, whales, wolves and more — which is why 'Ten solutions' is meant quite literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten solutions → COLLECTIVE NOUNS: the phrase names a grammatical class, and ten answers in this grid are members of it, so the definition points at the puzzle itself.

clue.text: Whack the top guy and stay mum (4)

blocks.note: the commanding officer is the man in charge of a unit
SH is the noise you make telling someone to keep quiet

explanation.walkthrough: CO for commanding officer is worth banking: it turns up whenever a clue mentions a boss, an officer or whoever is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Whack → COSH: to cosh somebody is to hit them with a heavy stick or bar, so it is one particular kind of whack.

clue.text: Begging your permission, tread carefully (4)

definitions.note: 'Pace' is the Latin preposition English borrowed — pace Dr Johnson — meaning 'with all respect to', which is why a whole polite phrase defines one short word.

blocks.note: the bookish word used before disagreeing with someone, by their leave
the plain English verb for walking in measured, deliberate steps

explanation.walkthrough: Two different words share one spelling — one straight out of Latin, one plain English — which is how the clue defines it twice without repeating itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin pace begs leave before contradicting someone; the English verb means to step out a distance deliberately, one measured stride at a time.

clue.text: Wild Bunch get ready to hit the road (4)

definitions.text: get ready to hit the road

blocks.note: wolves and hounds run in one

blocks.clueFragment: get ready to hit the road
blocks.note: filling a case is what you do before a journey

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point at the western film, which is the misdirection; the wolves' word is also one of the collective nouns this grid keeps turning up.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild bunch is what a pack of wolves running loose amounts to, and to pack is to fill your bags before setting off on a trip.

clue.text: See 24
Local, having no cash, in the clear (8)

blocks.note: your local is the pub, an inn
O is the round nothing, as written on a scoresheet
a cent is the smallest coin of American cash

explanation.walkthrough: Read the back half as a sum of money — nought cents, not a bean — and the penniless regular of the surface stops getting in the way.
explanation.definitionFit: in the clear → INNOCENT: somebody cleared of a charge is innocent of it, the courtroom verdict and the everyday phrase meaning the same thing.
